channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Five ways to look after yourself as winter approaches
item.description: When the clocks "fall back" in the fall, it signals the start of the winter months. And for many, this time change also signals the start of a difficult period—when the cold weather and long nights wear on their mental health.

item.title: Treatment revives old liver cells in lab study, may help prevent Alzheimer's and heart disease
item.description: The liver's job of clearing harmful substances from the body is so essential that the organ may have implications for addressing unexpected diseases, including Alzheimer's and heart disease. A promising example comes from new Keck School of Medicine of USC research published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry.

item.title: More education reduces dementia risk decades later
item.description: A law that required British teenagers to stay in school for an additional year had an unexpected consequence nearly 50 years later: fewer dementia diagnoses.

item.title: New zebrafish models could help test treatments for mental health conditions
item.description: A humble fish can experience features of mental health conditions such as schizophrenia and autism, raising the possibility that some of our most complex social behaviors may be more deeply encoded in our DNA than previously thought.

item.title: Adding abiraterone to ADT and docetaxel improves survival in metastatic prostate cancer
item.description: Adding abiraterone to standard treatment provides a lasting survival benefit for men whose prostate cancer has already spread at diagnosis, reinforcing the value of early treatment intensification. The findings come from almost eight years of follow-up in the academically led phase 3 PEACE-1 trial presented at the ESMO Congress 2026.

item.title: Omega-3 EPA linked to longer survival after surgery for colorectal cancer liver metastases
item.description: Patients assigned to receive high-dose eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), an omega-3 fatty acid, before and after surgery for colorectal cancer liver metastases had longer overall survival than those assigned to receive placebo, according to results of the phase 3 EMT2 trial presented at the ESMO Congress 2026, held in Madrid Oct. 23–27.

item.title: Fast-aging placentas may explain preeclampsia risks
item.description: Preeclampsia affects up to 8% of pregnancies worldwide and contributes to about 16% of maternal deaths globally, making the condition one of pregnancy's most serious complications. For women diagnosed with preeclampsia, the only cure is often to deliver the baby—even if the pregnancy has not yet reached full term.

item.title: Study outlines comprehensive roadmap for AI in mental health care
item.description: Researchers from the Faculty of Social Sciences at The University of Hong Kong (HKU), in collaboration with international experts from the University of Cambridge; the University of California, Berkeley; the National University of Singapore and other institutions, have published a comprehensive roadmap for the future of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies in mental health. Published in the journal Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics, the article examines how these technologies can advance mental health care while balancing opportunities and risks, providing priorities for future research and implementation.

item.title: Medical education: How are residents using AI?
item.description: A new study led by Yale School of Medicine's Wendy Barr, M.D., M.P.H., has evaluated the use of artificial intelligence among more than 15,000 family medicine residency trainees across the U.S. and found that in October 2025, 71% of residents had used AI for work in the past month. The paper is published in the journal Family Medicine.

item.title: Weakness and mobility loss in aging are not just muscle problems
item.description: An older patient mentions that climbing the stairs has become harder. They have stopped carrying the groceries in from the car. Last month, they had a fall in the kitchen.

item.title: Multiomic atlas of the developing thalamus reveals how neuronal identities emerge
item.description: A team from the Institute for Neurosciences (IN), a joint center of the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) and Miguel Hernández University of Elche (UMH), has developed the first multiomic atlas of the mouse embryonic thalamus, providing a detailed reconstruction of how the different neuronal cell types in this brain region emerge during development.

item.title: Fewer US men are diagnosed with low-risk prostate cancer, and more of them now choose surveillance over treatment
item.description: An analysis of United States data reveals a broad shift away from overtreatment of low-risk prostate cancer. The analysis published in CANCER indicates a shift toward surveillance in response to concerns of overdiagnosis and overtreatment that have hindered screening in the recent past.

item.title: Substance use driving increases in emergency department visits, hospitalizations for young mothers
item.description: Emergency department (ED) visits for use of substances, especially opioids, amphetamines and cannabis, by mothers with dependent children increased almost 5% a year, in contrast to an increase of almost 2% a year among females without children, according to a large study in Canadian Medical Association Journal. These increases were largely in mothers under age 25, in whom rates grew more than four times faster than among other females.

item.title: Young adults with cancer report putting off appointments, getting dismissed by doctors
item.description: When Natasha Allard's close friend Dave was diagnosed with stage 4 testicular cancer at age 26, the University at Buffalo postdoctoral associate started paying more attention to how cancer was upending the lives of young people.

item.title: Cracking a smile regularly may be good not just for your mood but for your health
item.description: Reminding yourself to smile often can not only help you form more friendships but also make you feel better.

item.title: New animal model offers more precise way to study calorie-burning brown fat
item.description: Researchers at LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center have developed and validated a new genetic animal model that gives scientists a more precise way to study brown and beige fat, specialized tissues that use energy to produce heat and play an important role in metabolism. The paper is published in the journal Scientific Reports.

item.title: Can psychedelics soothe an overactive immune system? New meta-analysis investigates
item.description: The same substances that can alter perception and shift moods are now drawing scientific interest for their potential therapeutic abilities. Researchers across the globe are investigating whether psychedelics, such as psilocybin from magic mushrooms or LSD, could help treat mental health and brain-related disorders. In a recent study, researchers gathered many such studies and carried out a systematic review and meta-analysis focusing on the anti-inflammatory and immune-modulating properties of serotonergic psychedelics.

item.title: Postpartum recovery window may play a critical role in maternal aging and long-term health
item.description: In many studies, it appears that women who have more children have a higher risk of heart disease and a shorter life span, but this effect is inconsistent across populations and no good explanation for it exists. Against this backdrop, new tools to assess biological age—the age reflected by one's biological state, rather than simply the number of years they have been alive—have revealed that pregnancy temporarily elevates biological age, while postpartum recovery can return it closer to baseline.

item.title: Doubling stem cell chromosomes produces heart cells with stronger, faster contractions
item.description: The Regenerative Medicine Project at our institute is advancing therapeutic strategies for various diseases by introducing a range of modifications to human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells.

item.title: Advanced age does not limit the benefits of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors in chronic kidney disease
item.description: New research uncovers the potential benefits and risks of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors for adults aged 80 years or older with chronic kidney disease (CKD). The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

item.title: Ultrasonic technology enables earlier stress-fracture detection
item.description: Tibial stress fractures are among the most common overuse injuries affecting military personnel, but they can be difficult to identify in their earliest stages. Small stresses in the bone may develop before an injury becomes apparent through conventional diagnostic tools, creating a window of opportunity for earlier detection to enable intervention.

item.title: 10 years after Ebola in West Africa: Laboratory partnership improves viral hemorrhagic fever diagnostics in Guinea
item.description: Drawing on nearly a decade of surveillance, the researchers document the burden of Lassa fever in the region and explain how sustainable diagnostic structures can support prevention and help reduce the risk of major viral outbreaks.

item.title: Triple-action weekly weight-loss drug reduces sleep apnea in two late-stage trials
item.description: Sleep apnea often gets passed off as mere snoring, but it's a much bigger deal. Throughout the night, breathing keeps pausing, and each pause chips away at sleep quality. Left untreated, repeated breathing disruptions and drops in blood oxygen during sleep can do far more than leave you groggy in the morning—they can take a serious toll on long-term health.

item.title: Creating 'satellite maps' of thousands of proteins across tissue could transform drug therapies
item.description: Much like a satellite provides a full picture of Earth, a new technology can generate thousands of detailed "satellite maps" showing where individual proteins are located and distributed across an entire tissue in the body or brain.

item.title: Ebola vaccine trial begins in DR Congo
item.description: The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday, the head of the World Health Organization said.

item.title: Kenya announces 2nd Ebola death, a close relative of the first patient
item.description: Kenya's Health Ministry announced the country's second Ebola death Friday, saying a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first patient died after developing symptoms while in quarantine.

item.title: Investigational vaccine generates immune response to KRAS mutations in pancreatic cancer study
item.description: An investigational vaccine helped the immune system recognize and respond to mutations that drive most pancreatic cancers, according to results from a randomized phase 2 clinical trial led by Mayo Clinic researchers. The findings, published in Nature Medicine, will help researchers design a larger phase 3 clinical trial.

item.title: Once-daily oral icotrokinra outperforms placebo in ulcerative colitis
item.description: For patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, oral icotrokinra, a peptide that blocks the interleukin-23 receptor, yields a clinical response at week 12 significantly more often than placebo, according to a study published in the Oct. 15 issue of the New England Journal of Medicine.

item.title: Diagnostic test could help doctors refine prostate cancer treatment
item.description: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men—in 2013, it affected more than 1 million men across the world. The cancer does not behave the same way in every patient, and doctors have long faced a difficult balancing act between identifying patients who will benefit from more intensive treatment and those who may do just as well without it. Treating someone more aggressively than necessary is associated with increased side effects and poorer quality of life.

item.title: Reprogramming tumor microenvironment could improve prospects for treatment of pancreatic cancer
item.description: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive and difficult-to-treat cancers. One reason for its resistance to therapy is the dense tissue surrounding the tumor that acts as a protective barrier and suppresses the immune response. It is a complex tissue made of supporting cells, blood vessels and immune cells—the tumor microenvironment. In pancreatic cancer, this surrounding tissue accounts for up to 90% of the tumor mass.
